## TL;DR

Updated the installed-upgrade notice so a hand-run server is identified plainly and can be restarted from the dashboard. The UI starts a detached CLI helper; the helper runs `repoos restart --force` against the current project and port, allowing the existing restart implementation to verify the server, stop it, and relaunch it with its recorded host and replayable serve flags. The CLI now authenticates its local idle-status request using the server's existing loopback-only token, fixing the HTTP 401 seen when a terminal or same-machine agent invokes `repoos restart`. The existing supervised-service restart route is unchanged. The scoped RepoOS check passed after the restart route and UI tests were updated.

## Work and rationale

The restart engine in `src/core/server-restart.ts` already distinguishes managed services, external supervisors, and hand-run servers. Its hand-run path resolves the server's recorded port, host, and restart-relevant arguments while the old process is alive, stops the exact verified PID, and starts a detached replacement. That design allows the new UI action to use a well-tested CLI path instead of duplicating process discovery and restart logic in a server route.

A server cannot safely be responsible for killing itself and then continuing its own restart work. I added a small helper launcher in the update-status route that starts the CLI detached from the server process, with the project root as its working directory and the current serve port as an explicit filter. For a source checkout it uses the compiled CLI entry when needed; if that entry is missing or the helper cannot be launched, the route returns a specific reason and the single fallback command, `repoos restart`. The helper's CLI invocation uses `--force` because pressing **Restart now** in the dashboard is the user's explicit choice to interrupt active work. The notice shows current agent and check counts and explains that agents resume after the replacement server starts.

The UI uses the shared button and dialog components already in the update notice. The hand-run state now says the server was started by hand and offers **Restart now**. It does not display `launchctl`, `systemctl`, or an unrelated shell command. The existing launchd/systemd supervised flow continues to use the existing restart request and keeps its restart-when-idle and cancel behavior. The light and dark release-notice fixtures now represent the hand-run path so the notice capture exercises the changed state.

The CLI 401 was caused by `cmdRestart` making an authenticated API request without the local credential. The server already creates a mode-0600 token for local CLI clients and the auth middleware accepts it only over loopback without forwarded headers. `cmdRestart` now reads that token from the configured cache location and sends it with the idle-status request. This preserves the auth boundary while allowing same-user terminals and local agents to use the existing endpoint. The idle check still refuses active work by default, `--when-idle` still waits, and `--force` remains the explicit override.

I updated the user-facing restart guidance to describe the hand-run dashboard action and local token behavior, and corrected the architecture guide's stale recommendation to use plain `repoos serve` for a hand-run restart. The changes do not alter `repoos service` semantics or the #0214 restart-adoption behavior; durable agent work is still adopted by the replacement process according to the existing restart machinery.

## Approaches tried

I first traced the installed-upgrade status payload, the shared notice component, the CLI restart command, the service manager, and the existing restart tests. This showed that `manualCommand` came from a service-registry based hint, while the modal's unsupervised branch treated every such server as terminal-only. I replaced that branch with the helper action and retained a terminal fallback only for a helper startup failure.

I considered adding a second process-relaunch implementation directly to the web route. That would duplicate the CLI's PID verification, work warning, supervisor classification, serve-flag replay, and readiness wait. Instead, the route only starts a detached CLI helper and lets `repoos restart` own those decisions. The route helper is separately testable with injected process-launch dependencies and verifies the exact command, cwd, detached mode, and port.

I also followed the HTTP 401 from the CLI's idle check into the shared server authentication middleware. Since the middleware already has a narrowly scoped local-token mechanism, using the token was a smaller and safer fix than exempting restart status from authentication or introducing a separate auth mechanism.

## Challenges and blockers

The first scoped check found two tests that asserted the behavior being removed: copying a manual restart string for an unsupervised server, and returning HTTP 409 from the route when no supervisor was detected. I rewrote the UI assertion to verify that a hand-run server shows the restart action without printing a supervisor command, and changed restart helper coverage to check the detached CLI invocation directly. A first version of that test attempted to observe the process launcher through a module mock while the route's cached supervisor state could select the alternate branch; the direct helper test avoids depending on cached OS detection while still exercising the command construction.

The full changed-path suite is broad and took several minutes per pass. The first pass failed on the outdated expectations; after correcting them, the scoped run completed successfully. I did not run a live restart against a real server, so the report does not claim device-level or end-to-end process-relaunch proof. The helper path, route wiring, CLI token use, build, static checks, UI smoke, contrast audit, and documentation build were validated by the repository check.

## Key learnings

The distinction between a server's parent process and a real supervisor service matters to restart UX. A terminal-launched server should not receive a fabricated service-manager command; it needs a real process outside the server to perform a verified stop and relaunch. The CLI already provides that orchestration and preserves the server's recorded options.

The local CLI token is the intended authentication mechanism for browser-less local commands. Any new CLI request to a protected local API must read and send it rather than weakening route authentication. Finally, tests around process routes should isolate command construction from environment-dependent supervisor detection; this keeps the branch-specific behavior deterministic without mocking the broader server lifecycle.
